content: Recommendations for an Acrylamide Standard 1. Technological Feasibility and Exposure Limits Current technology is sufficient to ensure compliance with the recommended acrylamide exposure standard. While the workplace environmental limit is considered safe based on available data, it should be treated as the maximum allowable exposure. Efforts must be made to minimize exposure to the lowest levels technically achievable. The criteria and standards will be reviewed and revised as necessary. 2. Terminology and Definitions Acrylamide is also referred to as propenamide, acrylic amide, or akrylamid. In this document, the terms acrylamide and acrylamide monomer are used interchangeably. The action level is defined as a time-weighted average (TWA) concentration equal to half the environmental limit. Occupational exposure to acrylamide includes working in areas where acrylamide is stored, produced, processed, or used, except when present as an unintentional contaminant at concentrations below 1% by weight. 3. Compliance Requirements If an employee is exposed to airborne acrylamide concentrations exceeding the action level, all sections of the recommended standard must be followed. If exposure is at or below the action level, all sections except Section 8 must be adhered to. Section 1: Environmental (Workplace Air) Concentration Control Employers must ensure that workplace acrylamide concentrations do not exceed the recommended limit. Procedures for collecting and analyzing environmental samples must follow the methods outlined in Appendices I and II or any equivalent method with comparable accuracy, precision, and sensitivity. Section 2: Medical Surveillance Preplacement Medical Examinations Before employment in areas with potential acrylamide exposure, individuals must undergo comprehensive medical and occupational history reviews, with emphasis on weight loss and neurological symptoms. A complete physical examination should focus on the skin, eyes, and nervous system. Additionally, the worker's ability to use respiratory protective equipment must be assessed. Periodic Examinations Annual medical examinations, or more frequent evaluations as determined by a physician, must be provided. These should include interim medical and work histories, weekly skin examinations for peeling or irritation, and physical examinations as outlined in the preplacement criteria. Emergency Medical Response In the event of acrylamide exposure, affected individuals must receive immediate first aid and medical attention, particularly for skin and eye contact. Medical personnel should monitor for delayed neurological effects. Contaminated clothing and shoes must be removed, and exposed skin should be thoroughly washed with soap and water. In cases of eye contact, eyes must be flushed with water, and a physician should be consulted promptly. Section 4: Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection Protective Clothing Workers must wear appropriate protective clothing, such as gloves, aprons, long-sleeved overalls, footwear, and face shields, to prevent skin contact with acrylamide. Impervious clothing may be required for specialized operations. Eye protection, such as chemical safety goggles or face shields, must be used in situations where acrylamide may contact the eyes. Respiratory Protection Engineering controls should be implemented to maintain acrylamide concentrations at or below the TWA limit. Respiratory protective equipment may be used during the installation or testing of engineering controls, emergencies, or nonroutine maintenance activities. Employers must provide and maintain respirators that meet NIOSH and MSHA standards and ensure employees are trained in their proper use and testing for leakage. Section 5: Informing Employees of Hazards Employee Training Employers must inform employees of the hazards of acrylamide exposure at the start of employment or upon assignment to an acrylamide area. Training should include symptoms of exposure (e.g., skin peeling, numbness, weakness, weight loss), emergency procedures, and safe handling practices. Maintenance and repair personnel must also be included in training programs. Employees should be reminded of these hazards annually and informed of the availability of relevant safety information, including material safety data sheets. Ventilation Systems Ventilation systems must be designed to prevent the accumulation or recirculation of acrylamide in the workplace, maintain concentrations at or below the recommended limit, and effectively remove acrylamide from employees' breathing zones. Regular maintenance and cleaning of ventilation systems are required to ensure their effectiveness. Emergency Procedures Preparedness and Response Employers must establish prearranged plans for obtaining emergency medical care and transporting injured workers. Employees should be trained in administering first aid and using approved protective equipment during cleanup operations. Nonessential personnel must be evacuated from exposure areas during emergencies, and hazardous areas must be clearly marked and secured. Monitoring and Recordkeeping If an employee is exposed to acrylamide above the recommended TWA limit, weekly exposure monitoring must be conducted until two consecutive measurements, at least one week apart, indicate compliance. Records of environmental monitoring must be maintained for at least 20 years. Acrylamide Production and Toxicity Production Methods Acrylamide is primarily produced from acrylonitrile through hydration processes. Advances in manufacturing have led to pollution-free methods for direct production of acrylamide monomer. The largest use of acrylamide is in the production of polyacrylamides for water treatment and other industrial applications. Toxicological Effects Acrylamide exposure has been associated with neurological symptoms, including motor incoordination and peripheral neuropathy, in both humans and animals. Acute exposure can result in convulsions and asphyxia, while chronic exposure may lead to sensory nerve damage. Studies in animals have demonstrated dose-dependent effects, with higher doses causing severe neurological and systemic toxicity. Human Case Studies Reports of acrylamide intoxication in workers have documented symptoms such as numbness, weakness, ataxia, and emotional changes. Recovery typically occurs after removal from exposure, though the duration of recovery varies. Neurological studies have shown that sensory nerves are more severely affected than motor nerves, with evidence of nerve degeneration and regeneration.
